conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can I confirm your name and date of birth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m Sarah Chen. My birthday is March 12, 2130.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Sarah. I see you’ve come in for worsening shortness of breath and to evaluate your tracheostomy. You’ve had this tube since you were three months old, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since I was a baby. I was born early, at 26 weeks, and my lungs never fully developed. I’ve had trouble breathing my whole life.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right, bronchopulmonary dysplasia from prematurity. And you’ve had four airway surgeries already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the last one was when I was about ten. They tried to remove the trach a few times, but I couldn’t breathe without it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Lately, you’ve been more short of breath, even at rest, and your cough has been worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s harder to do simple things like walking to the bathroom. And my sputum is sometimes green, but no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. We’re planning a rigid bronchoscopy today to look at your airway and possibly change your trach tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be under general anesthesia. The new tube will be fenestrated and uncuffed—Portex size 7 mm inside. That may help with speaking and airflow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it helps me breathe easier. I’m tired of feeling so winded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best. After the procedure, you’ll go to recovery, then back here to the floor. Your vitals look stable now—98% on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Sarah, you’re back from the OR. The bronchoscopy went well. We replaced your trach tube successfully and extubated you in the OR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I don’t remember much. Does it feel different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Too early to tell, but the airway looked better. We’ll keep monitoring. You’ll continue your nebulizers and pulmonary toilet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Sarah. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My throat feels really sore, and my voice is super hoarse. I can barely talk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s not uncommon after the procedure. We’re concerned about some swelling in your voice box. We may need a flexible bronchoscopy to check it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Swelling? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. We’ll do the scope tomorrow to get a better look. In the meantime, try to rest your voice as much as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try not to talk much. But what’s causing the swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be irritation from the tube or an infection. We’re starting you on fluconazole just in case it’s a fungal infection—thrush in the larynx.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, like a yeast infection in the throat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s more common in people with chronic airway issues. We’ll treat it for 14 days to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also started a higher dose of omeprazole. Your GERD might be contributing to the throat irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heartburn for years. Does that really affect my airway?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stomach acid can reflux up and irritate your larynx, especially when lying down. That’s why we want you to sit up during meals and keep your head elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure to do that at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Sarah. Ready for the flexible bronchoscopy this afternoon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess so. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation, so you’ll be relaxed. It’s to check the swelling we’re worried about—supraglottic edema.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Sarah, back from the scope. We saw significant swelling in your upper airway and signs of laryngitis. No obstruction, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what does that mean? Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It explains your hoarseness. We’ll keep you on fluconazole and voice rest. The swelling should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I ever get my voice back fully?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, yes. It just takes time and rest. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news, Sarah. Your voice is already a little stronger today. The swelling is starting to go down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried I’d lose my voice for good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also consulting thoracic surgery. They want to explore long-term options for your bronchopulmonary dysplasia—maybe a stent trial or more tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More surgery? I’ve already had so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. They’re just gathering info—pH testing for reflux, questionnaires. Nothing urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well overall. We think you can go home tomorrow if your breathing stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I miss my mom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with instructions: trach care as before, humidified air, and finish the full 14-day fluconazole course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lozenges for my throat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, menthol lozenges as needed. And liquid Tylenol for pain. No solid food for now—stick to soft or liquid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Sarah. You’re cleared to go home. Your breathing is stable, and your voice is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: head of bed elevated, sit up for meals, and follow up with your pulmonologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And finish all my meds, especially the fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take care, Sarah. Call if you have trouble breathing or your voice worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Dr. Patel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this is over. But I hope I don’t have to come back soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best to keep you stable. Your team will coordinate the next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your albuterol and acetylcysteine nebs as prescribed. And montelukast twice daily now—chewable tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. The dose changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we increased it to better control your asthma symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to take it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And the omeprazole twice daily now—to protect your throat from acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll set reminders. Don’t want another flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart plan. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Dr. Patel. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great, Sarah. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.
